questions.q: How many coats of paint do I need for a room?
questions.a: Two coats is the normal interior finish, and three when the colour changes sharply or the wall is patching bare plaster. The calculator applies the coats you choose and shows the litres for each one separately, so a single coat refresh is priced as a refresh. On a wall that has been skimmed, a mist coat first is usual practice, and it is priced as its own line because it consumes material without being part of the finish.

questions.q: How do I work out how much paint to buy for a room?
questions.a: Measure the walls you are painting, deduct the openings you are not painting, then divide by the coverage the product states. The calculator does the measuring arithmetic and the division, then rounds up to the tin sizes sold where you are working. Two things decide the answer more than the area does: the product's coverage, which differs widely between a premium emulsion and a contractor grade one, and whether you are changing colour, which costs an extra coat.

questions.q: Does the paint estimate include primer and undercoat?
questions.a: Yes, and on their own lines, with their own coverage and their own quantities. A primer or undercoat is a different product from a topcoat, consumed at a different rate, and pricing it as extra topcoat litres produces an order that is short on one and long on the other. If you are painting over a sound, previously painted wall, leave them out of the estimate and the total drops accordingly.

questions.q: What is not included in a paint estimate?
questions.a: Labour, masking, sanding, filling, caulking and any surface repair are outside this estimate, as are scaffolding and protection of floors and furniture. The estimate covers paint and primer quantities and their cost from the product records, which is the part you need before you go to the paint shop. It also leaves out any specialist product a substrate demands, because that is a specification decision rather than a quantity calculation.

questions.q: Does the calculator work in square feet?
questions.a: Switch the unit and the area, coverage and tin sizes all convert together, so a building measured in feet and a specification written in litres still produce one order. The conversion happens on the factors rather than on the final figure, so a square metre never becomes a scaled length. Enter coverage in the unit you are working in and the division stays in one system, which is what prevents the doubling errors that come from converting twice.

Wall and ceiling areas are measured separately because they take different products, openings are deducted because nobody paints a window, and the number of coats is yours to set because a refresh and a colour change are not the same job.

The arithmetic is deliberately plain. Area to be painted, divided by the coverage the product states, multiplied by the number of coats, rounded up to the tin sizes your market sells. What makes the result usable is not the division but the discipline around it: coverage comes from the product record instead of an assumed spread rate, primer is priced as its own product with its own consumption, and waste is a stated percentage rather than a silent margin added to the litres.

questions.q: How many tiles do I need for a floor or wall?
questions.a: Measure the floor or wall, then divide by the area of one tile, allowing for the joint if you want a close figure. The calculator does the division from the tile dimensions in millimetres or inches, so the count is in whole tiles and then converted to boxes. For a wall, measure each elevation separately and deduct the openings, because a room perimeter multiplied by height includes the door and window areas you are not tiling.

questions.q: Why does the tile calculator add a waste allowance?
questions.a: Because a tiled surface is not a rectangle. Edges need cuts, and cuts produce offcuts that cannot be used elsewhere. Tiles break in transit and on site, and a spare box left in the garage is what saves a matching problem when one cracks two years later. A straight lay in a large format needs around ten percent, a diagonal or herringbone layout needs fifteen or more, and the allowance is a percentage you set so it is visible in the total.

questions.q: How much tile adhesive and grout will I need?
questions.a: Adhesive follows the bed thickness and the coverage the product states, and grout follows the joint width, tile size and depth. The calculator asks for the coverage you are working to and multiplies it across the area, then converts to the bag size sold in your market. Grout is the one people underestimate: a small format tile with wide joints can consume several times the grout of a large format in the same area, so the calculator uses the geometry instead of a rate per square metre.

questions.q: Should I buy exactly the tiles the calculator shows?
questions.a: No. Buy the boxes the calculator shows, and keep the spare box. Tile production runs change shade, and a repair two years later needs a match that a new batch may not give. The boxes figure already includes the waste you set, so buying the raw area and hoping the cuts work out is how a job ends up one box short on a Friday afternoon.

questions.q: How do I allow for cuts, breakages and spares?
questions.a: Cuts at edges, breakages in transit and a spare for future repair are all waste, and waste is a percentage you control. Ten percent suits a straight lay, fifteen or more for a diagonal or herringbone, and more again for a room with many corners. It appears as its own line, so when a client asks why the order is larger than the floor area, the answer is a number on the page.

The calculator holds all three together so a job is not ordered in three separate trips to the merchant.

The mechanics are simple and unforgiving. Floor or wall area divided by the area of one tile gives the count, the layout pattern decides how much of that count is lost to cuts, and the tile size with the joint width decides how many square metres a bag of adhesive and a kilogramme of grout will serve. Because those relationships change with the pattern and the format, both stay as inputs you set, and the tool shows the square metres each bag covers rather than assuming one.

questions.q: How do I calculate how much POP I need for a ceiling?
questions.a: Multiply each room's length by its width for the area, then add the perimeter for the framing, and it is the second figure that a quick estimate usually forgets. The calculator takes the dimensions room by room, converts the total area into boards at the size you specify, and converts the total perimeter into screed, channel and trim. Compound then follows the joints the chosen board size creates, so a smaller board raises both the board count and the compound.

questions.q: Does the POP calculator account for the ceiling design?
questions.a: It uses the dimensions of the design you are building, so a simple flat ceiling is priced accurately and a design with steps, coves or curves needs those features measured as extra runs. Measurement is yours to take, and the arithmetic on top of it is the calculator's. That division matters on a decorated ceiling, because the design detail is geometry rather than something a rate per square metre can carry.

questions.q: Are labour and scaffolding included in a POP ceiling estimate?
questions.a: They are not included. The estimate covers board, framing, compound, tape and trim, which is what you need to order before the work starts. Labour follows the design and the access, and scaffold depends on the ceiling height and what is underneath. Both are priced separately, and putting them into a material estimate produces a number that is accurate for neither.

questions.q: Can I estimate a POP ceiling by room count instead of area?
questions.a: Not reliably. Two rooms of the same count can differ by several square metres and by more in perimeter, which is what drives the framing. Entering each room's length and width takes a minute and gives an area and a perimeter the estimate can actually use. A room count is a budgeting shorthand, and the calculator is designed to replace it with the measurement the order depends on.

questions.q: How is the perimeter used in a POP estimate?
questions.a: Screed, channel and trim follow the perimeter of each room, so a long narrow room needs more of all three than a square room of the same area. The calculator takes the perimeter from the dimensions you enter and prices the framing against it. This is why an estimate built from area alone under orders on circulation spaces, corridors and long living rooms, and why the perimeter appears as its own line.

A room count gets none of them right, and an area alone misses the framing entirely, which is where a ceiling budget usually goes wrong. The calculator takes each room's length and width, builds the area and the perimeter from them, and carries both into the quantities.

Ceilings are not floors. The area decides board and compound, the perimeter decides screed, channel and trim, and the height of the room decides nothing at all except the scaffold you will need. Because a long narrow room and a square room can share an area and differ by several metres of perimeter, the tool keeps the two measurements apart and prices each against its own rule.

questions.q: How much sand and cement do I need for a floor screed?
questions.a: Multiply the floor area by the thickness to get a volume, then split that volume by the mix ratio into sand and cement. The calculator does both steps and expresses cement in the bag size sold in your market, with sand by volume or by tonne. Two things move the answer more than the area does: the thickness, which multiplies everything, and the mix, because a one to three screed uses noticeably more cement than a one to five for the same volume.

questions.q: How thick should a floor screed be?
questions.a: Between forty and seventy five millimetres is common for a levelling screed over a prepared base, with thinner sections used for a wearing surface over a sound floor. Below about forty millimetres the risk of curling and debonding rises, and above seventy five the material cost climbs quickly. Those are specification judgements, so the calculator asks for your thickness and shows what it consumes rather than choosing one for you.

questions.q: Does a screeding estimate include the floor finish?
questions.a: No. Tile, stone, screed paint and any levelling compound above the screed are separate products with their own quantities and their own trades. The estimate covers the screed itself, which is what you order before the floor finish is even selected. Keeping them apart matters on a quotation, because a client changing the tile should not change the screed quantity, and mixing them makes that comparison impossible.

questions.q: What thickness should I enter for screeding?
questions.a: Enter the depth the specification calls for, in millimetres. If the base is uneven, the average depth is what governs the order, so measure the high and low points and use a figure that reflects the average rather than the minimum. The calculator shows the volume implied, which is the quickest way to sanity check whether the depth on a drawing meets the floor level you are trying to achieve.

questions.q: Does screeding cover a floor or a wall?
questions.a: Both, as separate surfaces, because they are measured and bought differently. A floor screed is a volume of sand and cement placed to a depth; a wall render is an area at a stated thickness, often with a different mix and a different finish. The calculator keeps the two apart so a wall is not ordered by the cubic metre and a floor is not priced from a render rate per square metre.

That is why thickness is the first input the tool asks for and why a change from forty to seventy millimetres changes the material by three quarters on the same floor.

The other half of the job is where the screed sits. A floor screed is ordered by volume, a wall render by area at a stated thickness, and a wearing surface over a sound base is thinner than a levelling screed over an uneven one. Keeping those cases apart is what stops a floor being priced at a render rate and a wall being ordered by the cubic metre.

questions.q: How much concrete do I need for a foundation?
questions.a: Multiply each footing run's length, width and depth, add the runs, then add the waste allowance you work to. The calculator does that from the dimensions you enter and shows the total before waste as well as after, so a checking engineer can see both. Cement, sand and coarse aggregate then follow from the mix you specify, expressed in the bag size and the units your market sells, so the order is something a supplier can price.

questions.q: How many blocks do I need for the foundation?
questions.a: Take the wall length, multiply by the height, divide by the face area of the block you are using, then deduct the openings and add waste. The calculator works from the block size you specify, which matters because a four hundred and fifty by two hundred and twenty five millimetre block and a four hundred and forty by two hundred and fifteen millimetre block do not cover the same area. Mortar follows the joint thickness and the wall area, so a thinner joint reduces both the mortar and the cement in it.

questions.q: Is this foundation design?
questions.a: No, and it says so on the page. Footing width, depth and reinforcement are structural design decisions that follow from the load and the ground, and a quantity tool cannot make them. When those dimensions come from your engineer, this tool converts them into a material order. When they do not exist yet, the useful next step is a soil report and a design, not a guessed footing width.

questions.q: Does the foundation estimate include formwork?
questions.a: No. Formwork, hardcore, blinding, damp proofing and excavation are separate items with their own quantities, and they are usually priced by a different trade. The estimate covers the concrete and the blockwork, which are the two materials you need to order before the first pour. Adding formwork to a concrete quantity produces a figure that reads as complete while leaving several real costs out of it.

questions.q: Does the foundation cost include tax?
questions.a: No. Tax is not determined in this estimate. Where a configured tax rule applies to your market, it appears as its own line with the basis stated; where no rule applies, the total is shown without tax rather than with an assumed percentage. That matters when you are comparing quotes from different regions, because a figure with an invented tax rate cannot be compared with one without it.

questions.q: What is a build-to-roof estimator?

questions.q: How many weep holes does a retaining wall need?

questions.q: What does the structural takeoff measure?
questions.a: It measures concrete and reinforcement for the elements you describe. Each slab, beam, column, footing or wall is entered with its own dimensions, and the quantities roll up by material. Reinforcement is counted by bar diameter, length and number, then converted to mass using the unit weight of that bar size, which is how a steel order is placed. What it does not do is decide the dimensions: those come from the structural design, and the schedule assumes they are already fixed.

questions.q: Where do the dimensions come from?
questions.a: From you, and from the drawing you are reading. The length, breadth and depth of each element are entered as they appear on the design, and the bar schedule supplies the diameters and lengths for reinforcement. The tool does not scale a drawing or infer a section from a span, because a takeoff built on inference is a takeoff that cannot be checked. Where a dimension is missing, it is reported as missing so the gap is closed on the drawing before anything is ordered.

questions.q: Is this a structural design?
questions.a: No. It is a material schedule, which is a different document from a design. Sizing members, calculating loads, checking deflection and detailing reinforcement are engineering work, and the tool assumes that work is done. The value it adds is turning a finished design into quantities and an order that can be placed, checked and audited, which is where most of the arithmetic and nearly all of the clerical error live.

questions.q: How are the concrete ingredients split?
questions.a: From the mix you specify, in proportions by volume, converted to the bag size sold in your market. A one to one and a half to three mix and a one to two to four mix give noticeably different cement content for the same concrete volume, so the mix is an input rather than a default. Sand and aggregate are then expressed by volume or by tonne, and cement by bag, because that is how each is bought at a merchant in most markets.

questions.q: Can I mix slabs, beams, columns and footings?
questions.a: Yes, and they should be, because a frame is placed and poured in sequence rather than in one operation. Each element keeps its own line with its own dimensions and quantity, and the materials roll up across the whole set. That way a slab can be ordered for one pour and columns for another, while the totals still tell you what the whole frame needs. Mixing everything into a single volume loses the sequence and makes a partial pour impossible to price.

article.summary: Concrete volumes and reinforcement quantities for the structural elements you survey.
article.description:
A structural takeoff is a schedule, not a design. Slabs, beams, columns, footings and walls are each measured from their own dimensions, and the totals roll up by material so the steel order and the concrete order are separate documents. The tool holds that shape because a concrete frame is bought as materials, not as elements.

What it will not do is decide the size of anything. A beam is measured at the depth it was designed to, a slab at its designed thickness, and the reinforcement counted in the diameters and lengths on the bar schedule. Those are the inputs. The output is the concrete volume, the formwork area where you ask for it, and the reinforcement weight by diameter, which is what a supplier and a fixer both work from.
functions: Measures each element type from its own dimensions: length, breadth and depth for a slab, section and length for a beam or column.

Six columns three metres high at three hundred by three hundred add one and six tenths. The total is close to sixteen cubic metres of concrete, and at a one to one and a half to three mix that is roughly five cubic metres of cement, seven and a half of sand and fifteen of aggregate, in bags and tonnes for your market. Reinforcement comes separately: twenty five bars of sixteen millimetre at seven metres, plus thirty of twelve millimetre at five metres, converted to kilogrammes by bar mass and summed by diameter, so the steel order is a schedule a fabricator can cut from.
advantages: Elements stay separate and materials roll up, which is the shape both a checking engineer and a supplier need.

questions.q: What does field sync do?
questions.a: It brings measurements and notes recorded on site back into the estimate, so a dimension taken at the wall does not have to be remembered and retyped later.

questions.q: What happens if a sync clashes with a stored figure?
questions.a: The clash is shown and you choose which value stands. Nothing is overwritten quietly, because the site figure and the drawing figure are both evidence.

questions.q: Does it work offline?
questions.a: Records can be captured and sent when a connection returns. The state of each record is shown so an unsent measurement is not mistaken for a saved one.

questions.q: Is it a project management tool?
questions.a: No. It moves measurements and notes between site and estimate. Task tracking and document control are separate.

questions.q: Who can see a synced record?
questions.a: Whoever has access to the estimate it belongs to, under the same permissions as the rest of the project.

questions.q: What does the material price page show?
questions.a: Current recorded prices per material and market, each with the date it was captured and the source it came from.

questions.q: Are these prices guaranteed?
questions.a: No. They are recorded figures with dates. A supplier quotation for your quantity is the authority, and the page says so.

questions.q: Why does the date matter?
questions.a: Because a price without a date cannot be judged. A figure from six months ago is history, and showing its date is what stops it being used as current.

questions.q: Can I see where a price came from?
questions.a: Yes. Each recorded price carries its source reference, so a figure can be checked against the supplier or the survey it came from.

questions.q: How does this relate to the calculators?
questions.a: The estimators use configured price data. Where a material has no verified price, the calculator asks you to enter one instead of assuming it.
